module.title: Regulations
module.description: FAA Part 107 rules and regulatory requirements for sUAS operations

lessons.title: General Regulations
objectives: Understand the applicability of 14 CFR Part 107 to sUAS operations
Define key terms: sUAS, Remote PIC, Visual Observer, Control Station
Know the 55-pound weight limit and what it includes
Know when a small unmanned aircraft must be registered and how it is marked
Explain the responsibility and authority of the remote PIC

sections.title: Applicability of Part 107
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR Part 107 governs the **registration, certification, and operation** of civil small unmanned aircraft systems within the United States.

**Part 107 applies to:**

- Civil (non-military, non-public) small UAS operations in the NAS
- Any sUAS weighing **less than 55 pounds** at takeoff (including everything on board)
- Both commercial and non-commercial operations conducted under Part 107
- Airman certification (your Remote Pilot Certificate)

**Part 107 does NOT apply to:**

- **Recreational flying** under 49 U.S.C. §44809 (TRUST test)
- **Public aircraft operations** (government operations under a COA)
- Operations under Section 333 or §44807 exemptions
- sUAS with an airworthiness certificate operating under Part 91

## Why It Matters

This is the first question you should answer: "Does Part 107 apply to what I'm doing?" If you're flying commercially (real estate photos, inspections, mapping, delivery), this regulation governs you.

## What the Exam Tests

Expect questions like:
- "Under what regulation would a commercial drone operation fall?"
- "A drone weighing 52 lbs with a camera is used for real estate photography. What regulations apply?"
- "Which operations are NOT covered by Part 107?"

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.3 defines the core terminology every remote pilot must know.

### Small Unmanned Aircraft

An unmanned aircraft weighing **less than 55 pounds on takeoff**, including everything on board or attached.

### Small Unmanned Aircraft System (sUAS)

The small unmanned aircraft **and its associated elements** — communication links, control components — required for safe operation.

> **Key Distinction:** The "aircraft" is just the flying machine. The "system" is the aircraft PLUS controller, data link, ground station, and display.

### Remote Pilot in Command (Remote PIC)

The person who holds a Remote Pilot Certificate with sUAS rating and has **final authority and responsibility** for the operation.

### Visual Observer (VO)

A person designated by the remote PIC to assist with see-and-avoid duties. VOs are **optional**, not required.

### Control Station

The interface (controller/tablet/GCS) used to control the flight path.

### Person Manipulating Flight Controls

Whoever is physically operating the sticks at any moment. May or may not be the Remote PIC.

## Why It Matters

These definitions establish the **chain of responsibility**. The Remote PIC holds final authority — even if someone else is flying the drone.

bogeyman.message: Aircraft versus system: the aircraft is just the drone. The sUAS is the aircraft plus the controller, data links, and everything else needed to operate it.

sections.title: The 55-Pound Weight Limit
sections.content:
## What the Rule Says

The maximum takeoff weight for a small unmanned aircraft under Part 107 is **less than 55 pounds**, including:

- The aircraft itself
- All batteries
- All payload (cameras, sensors, cargo)
- Any attachments (parachute systems, lights)

## Common Traps

- If your drone weighs 48 lbs and you attach a 10 lb camera, that's 58 lbs — **no longer qualifies** under Part 107
- The weight is measured at **takeoff**, not empty weight
- Part 107 is not only for paid work. Any flight that is not strictly recreational falls under it, and a recreational flyer may choose to fly under it

## Key Facts to Memorize

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Maximum takeoff weight | **< 55 lbs** (including all onboard equipment) |
| Governing regulation | **14 CFR Part 107** |
| Recreational alternative | 49 U.S.C. §44809 (TRUST test) |
| Public aircraft | Excluded — operate under COA |

sections.title: Registration and Marking
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.13 requires every small unmanned aircraft flown under Part 107 to be registered. Registration and marking for aircraft under 55 pounds are covered by **14 CFR Part 48**.

## Who Must Register

| Type of flying | Aircraft weight | Registration required? |
|---|---|---|
| Part 107 | Any weight under 55 lbs | **Yes** |
| Strictly recreational (49 U.S.C. 44809) | 0.55 lbs or less | No |
| Strictly recreational (49 U.S.C. 44809) | More than 0.55 lbs | Yes |

The 0.55-pound exception in 14 CFR 48.15 covers only aircraft flown **exclusively** under the recreational exception. A 200-gram drone used for paid work must be registered.

## Key Facts

- Under Part 107, **each aircraft** is registered individually.
- A registration **expires 3 years** after it is issued and must be renewed (14 CFR 48.100).
- If the owner is under 13, a person who is at least 13 must register the aircraft (14 CFR 48.25).
- Registration information must be updated within 14 calendar days of a change (14 CFR 48.115).

## Marking

- The registration number must be **legibly displayed on an external surface** of the aircraft (14 CFR 48.205).
- It must stay attached for the whole flight.
- A number hidden inside a battery compartment does not meet the rule.

## Common Traps

- "Under 0.55 lbs never needs registration." Wrong for any Part 107 flight.
- "Registration lasts 24 months." Wrong. 24 calendar months is the pilot's knowledge recency period. Registration lasts 3 years.

bogeyman.message: The 0.55-pound number belongs to recreational flyers and to Category 1. It never excuses a Part 107 aircraft from registration.

sections.title: The Remote Pilot in Command
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.19 puts one person in charge of every flight.

- A remote pilot in command (remote PIC) must be **designated before or during the flight**.
- The remote PIC is **directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to,** the operation.
- The remote PIC must ensure the aircraft will pose **no undue hazard** to other people, other aircraft, or property if control is lost for any reason.
- The remote PIC must ensure the operation complies with all applicable regulations.
- The remote PIC must have the **ability to direct** the aircraft to ensure compliance.

## Letting Someone Else Fly

14 CFR 107.12 allows a person with no Remote Pilot Certificate to manipulate the flight controls only if that person is **under the direct supervision of a remote PIC who can immediately take direct control** of the aircraft.

The remote PIC stays responsible for the flight the whole time.

## Why It Matters

Responsibility does not move to the client, the aircraft owner, the visual observer, or whoever is holding the sticks. If the question asks who is responsible, the answer is the remote PIC.

## Common Traps

- "The visual observer shares final authority." No. The observer assists.
- "The owner of the drone is responsible for the flight." No. The remote PIC is.
- "A client can fly if they stay low and close." Altitude and distance are not the test. Direct supervision and the ability to take over immediately are.

lessons.title: Falsification and Accident Reporting
objectives: Understand consequences of falsifying records
Know when accident reporting is required
Memorize the 10-day deadline and $500 threshold

sections.title: Falsification of Records
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

Since **November 3, 2025**, the falsification rules for FAA regulations, including Part 107, are in **14 CFR 3.403**. The former section 107.5 is now reserved. Older study material still cites 107.5; the prohibited conduct is the same.

Under 14 CFR 3.403, no person may:

- Make or cause to be made any **fraudulent or intentionally false statement** in an application, record, report, or other document submitted to the FAA or kept to show compliance
- **Produce, reproduce, or alter** such a document for a fraudulent purpose
- **Knowingly omit** a material fact

## The Consequences

A violation is a basis for:

1. **Denying** an application for a certificate, rating, or authorization
2. **Suspending or revoking** any certificate, rating, or authorization the FAA has issued to that person
3. A **civil penalty**

## Why It Matters

Every accident report, training record, and certificate exists so the FAA and other pilots can rely on it. The sanction reaches every FAA certificate the person holds, not only the Remote Pilot Certificate.

## Common Traps

- The rule covers records you "cause to be made," not only ones you create yourself
- Changing a date on a training certificate is an alteration, however small
- There is no grace period that makes an altered record acceptable

sections.title: Accident Reporting Requirements
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

Under 14 CFR 107.9, the remote PIC must report to the FAA **no later than 10 calendar days** after any operation that results in:

1. **Serious injury** to any person, or **any loss of consciousness**
2. **Damage to any property other than the small UAS**, unless the cost of repair (materials and labor) is **$500 or less**, or, for a total loss, the fair market value of the property is **$500 or less**

AC 107-2A describes a serious injury as one rated level 3 or higher on the Abbreviated Injury Scale, for example an injury that requires hospitalization.

## The Report

The report goes to the FAA and describes:

- Date, time, and location of the event
- The remote PIC and the small UAS involved
- What happened
- Injuries or property damage

## What to Remember

1. The $500 threshold applies to property **other than** the drone
2. For a total loss, compare the property's **fair market value** to $500, not the repair cost
3. The deadline is **10 calendar days**, not business days
4. Any loss of consciousness triggers a report, even with no visible injury

bogeyman.message: The $500 threshold applies to property OTHER than your drone. If your $3,000 drone is destroyed but nothing else is damaged and nobody is hurt, there is nothing to report.

sections.title: Accident Reporting Scenarios
sections.content:
## Typical Exam Questions

**Scenario 1:** Your sUAS crashes into a parked car causing $600 in damage. The drone is destroyed ($1,200). No injuries.

→ **Report within 10 days.** Car damage exceeds $500; drone damage doesn't count.

**Scenario 2:** Your sUAS clips a tree and crashes. The $1,200 drone is totaled. No other damage, no injuries.

→ **No report required.** Damage to the sUAS itself is excluded.

**Scenario 3:** A bystander is hit by your sUAS and briefly loses consciousness but has no visible injuries.

→ **Yes, report it.** Loss of consciousness is a mandatory trigger regardless of visible injury.

**Scenario 4:** Your sUAS hits an old lawn tractor. Repair would cost $600, but the tractor's fair market value is only $200. No injuries.

→ **No report required.** For a total loss, the fair market value is what counts, and it does not exceed $500.

## Key Facts to Memorize

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Reporting deadline | **10 calendar days** |
| Property damage threshold | Repair cost over $500, or fair market value over $500 for a total loss (property OTHER than the sUAS) |
| Injury trigger | Serious injury to any person |
| Consciousness trigger | **Any loss of consciousness** |
| Drone damage | **Does NOT trigger reporting** |
| Report to | **FAA** |

bogeyman.message: 10 calendar days, not business days. Weekends and holidays count.

lessons.title: Operating Rules
objectives: State the preflight, fitness, and safe-condition duties of the remote PIC
Apply the rules on hazardous operation, moving vehicles, alcohol, and in-flight emergencies
Explain visual line of sight and the role of a visual observer
Recall the speed, altitude, visibility, and cloud clearance limits with their units
Describe the requirements for civil twilight and night operations
Know when ATC authorization or agency permission is required
Identify what the FAA and law enforcement may ask to see or inspect

sections.title: Safe Condition, Fitness, and Preflight
sections.content:
## Condition for Safe Operation (14 CFR 107.15)

- No one may operate a small UAS unless it is in a **condition for safe operation**.
- The remote PIC must check the system **before each flight**.
- No one may continue a flight after knowing, or having reason to know, that the system is no longer safe.

## Medical Condition (14 CFR 107.17)

No person may manipulate the flight controls, act as remote PIC, act as visual observer, or directly participate in the operation if that person **knows or has reason to know** of a physical or mental condition that would interfere with safe operation.

Part 107 requires no FAA medical certificate. Each crew member is responsible for an honest self-assessment, and the rule covers the whole crew, not only the remote PIC.

## Preflight Familiarization (14 CFR 107.49)

Before flight, the remote PIC must:

1. **Assess the operating environment**, including:
   - Local weather conditions
   - Local airspace and any flight restrictions
   - The location of persons and property on the surface
   - Other ground hazards
2. **Brief everyone directly participating** on the operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards
3. Ensure all **control links** between the control station and the aircraft are working properly
4. Ensure there is **enough power** to operate for the intended time
5. Ensure anything attached or carried is **secure** and does not adversely affect flight characteristics or controllability
6. For operations over people, ensure the aircraft meets the requirements of the category being used

## Common Traps

- "The aircraft was inspected this morning." The check is required before each flight.
- "Only the pilot has to be fit." The visual observer and other direct participants are covered too.
- "The briefing is optional for an experienced crew." It is required by 107.49.

bogeyman.message: 'Before each flight' means every flight, including the second battery of the day.

sections.title: Hazardous Operations and In-Flight Emergencies
sections.content:
## Careless or Reckless Operation (14 CFR 107.23)

No person may:

- Operate a small UAS in a **careless or reckless manner** that endangers the life or property of another
- **Drop an object** from a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that creates an **undue hazard** to persons or property

Dropping an object is not banned outright. It is allowed when it creates no undue hazard, and no waiver is involved.

## Moving Vehicles and Aircraft (14 CFR 107.25)

| Operating from | Allowed? |
|---|---|
| A moving aircraft | **Never** |
| A moving land or water vehicle | Only if the aircraft is flown over a **sparsely populated area** and is **not carrying another person's property for compensation or hire** |

## Hazardous Material (14 CFR 107.36)

A small unmanned aircraft may not carry hazardous material. This rule cannot be waived.

## One Aircraft at a Time (14 CFR 107.35)

No person may manipulate flight controls, or act as remote PIC or visual observer, for **more than one unmanned aircraft at the same time**. A visual observer or an automated mission does not change the limit. This rule can be waived.

## In-Flight Emergency (14 CFR 107.21)

- In an in-flight emergency that requires immediate action, the remote PIC may **deviate from any rule of Part 107 to the extent necessary** to meet that emergency.
- A remote PIC who deviates must send a **written report to the FAA only if the FAA requests one**.

The rule covers an emergency that arises during a flight. It is not permission to plan a flight outside the rules.

## Common Traps

- "Nothing may ever be dropped from a drone." Wrong. The test is undue hazard.
- "Flying from a moving truck is always illegal." Wrong. It depends on the area and on whether property is carried for hire.
- "Every emergency deviation must be reported within 10 days." Wrong. That deadline belongs to accident reporting under 107.9.

bogeyman.message: A deviation report is owed only if the FAA asks for it. Don't confuse it with the 10-day accident report.

sections.title: Alcohol and Drugs
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.27 applies the manned-aircraft alcohol and drug rules, 14 CFR 91.17 and 91.19, to the person manipulating the flight controls, the remote PIC, and the visual observer.

Under 14 CFR 91.17, no person may act as a crew member:

| Limit | Detail |
|---|---|
| Time | Within **8 hours** after consuming any alcoholic beverage |
| Influence | While **under the influence** of alcohol |
| Drugs | While using **any drug** that affects the person's faculties in any way contrary to safety |
| Concentration | With an alcohol concentration of **0.04 or greater** in a blood or breath specimen |

**Each limit stands alone.** Passing one does not excuse another.

14 CFR 91.19 also applies: no one may operate with knowledge that narcotic drugs, marijuana, or depressant or stimulant drugs are carried in the aircraft, unless authorized by law.

## Testing

A crew member must submit to an alcohol test when a law enforcement officer requests one under 91.17. Refusing has its own consequences, covered in the certification lesson.

## Common Traps

| Wrong idea | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| "The limit is 0.08" | That is a driving limit. The aviation limit is 0.04 |
| "The rule is 12 hours" | The regulation says 8 hours |
| "Under 0.04 means I can fly" | Not if fewer than 8 hours have passed, or if you are still under the influence |
| "Only prescription drugs count" | Any drug that affects your faculties counts, including over-the-counter medicine |

bogeyman.message: Eight hours, under 0.04, and not impaired. Miss any one of the three and you stay on the ground.

sections.title: Visual Line of Sight and Visual Observers
sections.content:
## Visual Line of Sight (14 CFR 107.31)

With vision **unaided by any device other than corrective lenses**, the crew must be able to see the aircraft **throughout the entire flight** in order to:

1. Know the aircraft's location
2. Determine its attitude, altitude, and direction of flight
3. Observe the airspace for other traffic or hazards
4. Determine that it does not endanger the life or property of another

That ability must be exercised by either:

- The remote PIC and the person manipulating the flight controls, **or**
- A visual observer

## What Does Not Count

- Binoculars or a telescope
- First-person-view goggles
- The camera feed on the controller

Eyeglasses and contact lenses are fine. AC 107-2A notes that binoculars may be used briefly to improve situational awareness, but they cannot be the means of keeping the aircraft in sight.

## Visual Observers (14 CFR 107.33)

A visual observer is optional. When one is used:

- The remote PIC, the person at the controls, and the observer must maintain **effective communication at all times**
- The remote PIC must ensure the observer can see the aircraft as 107.31 requires
- The crew must coordinate to scan the airspace for collision hazards and keep track of the aircraft's position by direct visual observation

AC 107-2A notes that devices such as hand-held radios may be used for crew communication.

## Common Traps

- "FPV goggles are fine if telemetry is shown." Not unless a visual observer keeps the aircraft in unaided sight.
- "The observer only needs to watch when the pilot loses sight." The requirement is continuous.
- "Staying within 400 feet of the pilot satisfies line of sight." Distance is not the test. Seeing the aircraft is.

bogeyman.message: A screen is not line of sight. If nobody on the crew can see the aircraft with their own eyes, the flight is outside the rule.

sections.title: Operating Limitations
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.51 sets four limits that apply in every class of airspace.

| Limit | Value | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Groundspeed | **87 knots (100 mph)** | Measured as groundspeed, not airspeed |
| Altitude | **400 feet AGL** | Higher only within a 400-foot radius of a structure, and then no more than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit |
| Visibility | **3 statute miles** | Observed from the location of the control station |
| Cloud clearance | **500 feet below** and **2,000 feet horizontally** | Applies in all airspace, including Class G |

Flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects can be seen and identified by day, and prominent lighted objects by night.

## Worked Examples

**Structure:** A tower stands 1,200 feet AGL. Flying within 400 feet of it, the aircraft may go as high as 1,200 + 400 = **1,600 feet AGL**. Away from the tower, the limit is 400 feet AGL again.

**Clouds:** The base of a cloud layer is 700 feet AGL. The aircraft must stay 500 feet below it: 700 - 500 = **200 feet AGL**. The cloud rule is more restrictive than the 400-foot rule here.

**Terrain:** An aircraft at 350 feet AGL flies off the edge of a plateau where the ground drops 300 feet. Without descending, it is now **650 feet AGL** and above the limit. Altitude is measured from the ground directly below the aircraft, not from the launch point.

**Speed:** A fixed-wing aircraft shows 95 knots groundspeed with a tailwind. That exceeds 87 knots, whatever its airspeed.

## Common Traps

| Wrong idea | Correct |
|---|---|
| The speed limit is 100 knots | 87 knots, which is 100 **miles per hour** |
| The 400-foot limit is MSL | It is AGL |
| Visibility is 3 nautical miles | 3 **statute** miles |
| Class G only needs "clear of clouds" | That is a manned-aircraft rule. Part 107 uses 500 below and 2,000 horizontal everywhere |
| An airspace authorization relaxes these limits | It satisfies the airspace rule only |

All four limits can be waived.

bogeyman.message: Read the unit before the number: knots or mph, AGL or MSL, statute or nautical.

sections.title: Daylight, Civil Twilight, and Night
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.29 allows flight during civil twilight and at night without a waiver when its conditions are met.

| Period | When (outside Alaska) | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Day | Official sunrise to official sunset | Nothing additional |
| Civil twilight | 30 minutes before official sunrise until sunrise, and sunset until 30 minutes after official sunset | Lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least **3 statute miles** |
| Night | From the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight | The same lighting, **and** the remote PIC must have completed an initial knowledge test or training under 107.65 after April 6, 2021 |

In Alaska, civil twilight is the period defined in the Air Almanac.

## The Anti-Collision Light

- Must be visible for at least 3 statute miles
- Must have a **flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision**
- The remote PIC **may reduce the intensity, but may not extinguish it**, if doing so is in the interest of safety because of operating conditions

## Worked Example

Official sunset is 7:30 p.m. A flight that continues until 7:50 p.m. is in evening civil twilight, so the anti-collision light must be on. After 8:00 p.m. it is night, and the training requirement applies as well.

## Common Traps

- "Night flight needs a waiver." That was the rule before April 2021. It is not the rule now.
- "Civil twilight counts as daytime, so no light is needed." The light is required during civil twilight.
- "Position lights or a steady light satisfy the rule." The rule calls for anti-collision lighting with a flash rate.
- "The light may be switched off if it bothers the pilot." It may be dimmed, never extinguished.

bogeyman.message: Twilight needs the light. Night needs the light and the training. Neither needs a waiver.

sections.title: Right of Way and Flying Near Airports
sections.content:
## Right of Way (14 CFR 107.37)

- A small unmanned aircraft must **yield the right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles**.
- Yielding means giving way. The aircraft may not pass over, under, or ahead of the other aircraft unless well clear.
- No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a **collision hazard**.

A drone never has the right of way over a manned aircraft. When two drones converge, neither has priority by weight or launch order, and both remote pilots must avoid a collision.

## See and Avoid

The remote PIC is responsible for seeing other aircraft first and moving away early. Do not count on the pilot of a manned aircraft seeing a small drone.

## Operating Near Airports (14 CFR 107.43)

No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that **interferes with operations and traffic patterns** at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base.

Part 107 has no fixed distance from an airport and no rule requiring notice to the airport manager. Whether ATC authorization is needed depends on the class of airspace, covered in the next section.

## Common Traps

- "The drone was there first, so the airplane must go around." Wrong. The drone yields.
- "Climb above the approaching aircraft." Wrong. Move away and, if needed, descend or land.
- "Part 107 pilots must stay 5 miles from airports." There is no such rule in Part 107.

sections.title: Airspace Authorization, Restricted Areas, and NOTAMs
sections.content:
## Controlled Airspace (14 CFR 107.41)

No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in:

- Class B airspace
- Class C airspace
- Class D airspace
- The lateral boundaries of the **surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport**

unless that person has **prior authorization from Air Traffic Control**.

Authorization is requested through **LAANC** or **FAADroneZone**. It is not obtained by calling the tower on the radio. Class G airspace, and Class E airspace that does not reach the surface around an airport, need no authorization.

## Prohibited and Restricted Areas (14 CFR 107.45)

No person may operate in a prohibited or restricted area without **permission from the using or controlling agency**. LAANC does not grant this.

## Flight Restrictions Issued by NOTAM (14 CFR 107.47)

The remote PIC must comply with temporary flight restrictions and other restrictions issued by NOTAM under 14 CFR 91.137 through 91.145 and 99.7. Flying below 400 feet or in Class G airspace gives no relief from a temporary flight restriction.

## Authorization Is Not a Waiver

An airspace authorization satisfies 107.41 and nothing else. Altitude, visibility, cloud clearance, and every other Part 107 rule still apply. Relief from those rules requires a certificate of waiver.

## Common Traps

- "Contact the tower by radio before entering Class D." That is the manned-aircraft rule.
- "All Class E airspace needs authorization." Only the surface area designated for an airport.
- "A waiver for altitude also covers the airspace." It does not. Authorization is separate.

The Airspace module covers how to identify each of these on a chart.

sections.title: Automation, Carrying Property, and Transponders
sections.content:
## Automated Flight

Part 107 allows automated flight, such as a pre-programmed mapping grid. Under 14 CFR 107.19 the remote PIC must still have the **ability to direct the aircraft** to ensure compliance, which means being able to change the flight path or take over. Visual line of sight and see-and-avoid apply exactly as they do in manual flight.

## Carrying Property for Compensation or Hire

Part 107 allows a remote pilot to carry another person's property for pay within these limits:

- The aircraft and everything it carries weigh **less than 55 pounds** in total
- The flight stays **within visual line of sight**
- The flight is **not conducted from a moving vehicle or aircraft**
- AC 107-2A adds that the flight must stay **within the bounds of a State**
- No hazardous material is carried

Waivers of the moving-vehicle rule (107.25) and the line-of-sight rule (107.31) cannot be used to carry another person's property for compensation or hire (14 CFR 107.205).

## Transponders and ADS-B Out

| Equipment | Rule |
|---|---|
| ATC transponder | May not be operated with the transponder on unless otherwise authorized by the FAA (14 CFR 107.52) |
| ADS-B Out | May not be operated in transmit mode unless otherwise authorized by the FAA (14 CFR 107.53) |

Neither prohibition depends on airspace or altitude. ADS-B Out also cannot be used to meet the Remote ID requirement.

## Common Traps

- "Automated missions do not need a pilot watching." They do.
- "Adding ADS-B Out makes the drone safer and is encouraged." Transmitting is prohibited without authorization.
- "Package delivery can go beyond line of sight with a waiver." Not when carrying another person's property for hire.

sections.title: Inspection and Compliance
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.7 covers what you must carry, what you must show, and what the FAA may inspect.

### Carrying and Showing Your Certificate

- When exercising the privileges of the certificate, you must have your **Remote Pilot Certificate and identification** in your physical possession and readily accessible.
- You must present them on request from:
  - The FAA
  - An authorized representative of the **NTSB**
  - Any **Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer**
  - An authorized representative of the **TSA**
- You must make available to the FAA, on request, any document, record, or report that the regulations require you to keep.

### Testing and Inspection

On request, the remote PIC, visual observer, owner, operator, or person manipulating the flight controls must allow the FAA to **test or inspect** the small UAS and the people involved, to determine compliance.

## Why It Matters

This is the legal basis for an inspector or a police officer approaching you in the field.

## Common Traps

- "Only FAA inspectors may ask to see the certificate." Wrong. Law enforcement, NTSB, and TSA may as well.
- "An officer needs a warrant." The rule requires you to present the certificate on request.
- The obligation is not only the remote PIC's. Observers, owners, and operators must also allow inspection.

sections.title: Multiple Category sUAS
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

A single sUAS can be eligible to operate under **more than one category** for operations over people (Categories 1–4). The same drone might qualify as Category 1 for one mission and Category 2 for another, depending on configuration.

**Critical Rule:** The Remote PIC must **not be able to inadvertently switch** between categories during flight.

## Why It Matters

Many commercial drones can be configured differently depending on the mission. A drone weighing 0.50 lbs with no payload (Category 1) might weigh 2 lbs with a camera attached (potentially Category 2 or 3).

## Key Facts

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Can one sUAS qualify for multiple categories? | **Yes** |
| What determines the category? | Configuration at time of operation |
| Key safety requirement | Cannot **inadvertently switch** categories during flight |

sections.title: Record Retention
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.165 establishes record retention requirements.

### For Manufacturers (Category 2/3 Aircraft)

- Must retain all supporting information demonstrating compliance
- Retention period: **2 years after ceasing production** of that model

### For Declaration Submitters

- Must retain all detailed information submitted with the declaration
- Retention period: **2 years after submission date**

### For Means of Compliance (MoC) Submitters

- Must retain the detailed description of the means of compliance
- Retention period: **As long as the MoC remains FAA-accepted**

### For All Remote Pilots (Best Practices)

While not mandated, the FAA strongly recommends maintaining:
- Flight logs
- Maintenance records
- Preflight inspection records
- Incident/accident documentation

## Key Facts to Memorize

| Who | Retention Period |
|---|---|
| Manufacturers (Cat 2/3) | **2 years** after ceasing production |
| Declaration submitters | **2 years** after submission date |
| MoC submitters | **As long as MoC remains FAA-accepted** |

lessons.title: Remote Pilot Certification
objectives: List the eligibility requirements for a Remote Pilot Certificate
Explain the 24-calendar-month recency requirement and how it is met
Know how alcohol or drug offenses and test refusals affect a certificate
Identify which Part 107 rules can be waived and how a waiver is requested

sections.title: Eligibility and Recency
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

Under 14 CFR 107.61, to be eligible for a Remote Pilot Certificate with a small UAS rating you must:

1. Be at least **16 years old**
2. Be able to **read, speak, write, and understand English**
3. Not know, or have reason to know, of a **physical or mental condition** that would interfere with safe operation
4. **Demonstrate aeronautical knowledge** by either:
   - Passing the initial aeronautical knowledge test, or
   - If you hold a Part 61 pilot certificate (other than a student pilot certificate) and have a current flight review, completing the FAA's initial training course

You may take the knowledge test at **14**, but the certificate is not issued until you are 16. After you apply, the TSA completes a security background check before the certificate is issued.

## After You Pass

- A temporary certificate is valid for up to **120 calendar days** while the permanent one is processed (14 CFR 107.64).
- If your permanent mailing address changes, you must notify the FAA **within 30 days**, or you may not exercise the privileges of the certificate (14 CFR 107.77).

## Recency (14 CFR 107.65)

To act as remote PIC, you must have done one of these **within the previous 24 calendar months**:

- Passed the initial knowledge test
- Completed **recurrent training**
- For Part 61 pilots with a current flight review, completed the Part 61 training course

Recurrent training is online and free. There is no recurrent test at a testing center, and the certificate itself **does not expire**.

"Calendar months" run to the end of the month. A test passed on March 10, 2025 keeps you current through March 31, 2027.

## Common Traps

- "The certificate expires after two years." It does not. Your recency does.
- "Recurrent knowledge tests are required." They were before April 2021. Recurrent training replaced them.
- "You must be 16 to take the test." You must be 14 to test and 16 to hold the certificate.

sections.title: Alcohol and Drug Offenses
sections.content:
## Offenses Involving Alcohol or Drugs (14 CFR 107.57)

Either of the following is grounds for **denying an application** for a Remote Pilot Certificate for up to **1 year**, or for **suspending or revoking** a certificate:

- A **conviction** under any Federal or State statute relating to narcotic drugs, marijuana, or depressant or stimulant drugs. The offense does not need to involve an aircraft.
- Committing an act prohibited by 14 CFR 91.17(a) or 91.19(a), such as acting as a crew member within 8 hours of drinking.

## Refusing a Test (14 CFR 107.59)

Either of the following is also grounds for denial for up to 1 year, or for suspension or revocation:

- **Refusing to submit to an alcohol test** when requested by a law enforcement officer
- **Refusing to furnish or authorize the release of test results** requested by the FAA

## Common Traps

- "A drug conviction unrelated to flying does not affect the certificate." It can.
- "Refusing the test avoids a violation." Refusal is itself grounds for suspension or revocation.

sections.title: Waivers
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

Under 14 CFR 107.200, the FAA may issue a **certificate of waiver** that allows a deviation from certain Part 107 rules if it finds the proposed operation can be conducted safely.

A waiver request must contain:

- A **complete description** of the proposed operation
- A **justification** showing the operation can safely be conducted under the terms of a waiver

The FAA may add limitations. The holder may deviate only as the waiver describes and must follow its conditions.

## Which Rules Can Be Waived (14 CFR 107.205)

| Section | Subject |
|---|---|
| 107.25 | Operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft |
| 107.29(a)(2) and (b) | Anti-collision lighting at night and in civil twilight |
| 107.31 | Visual line of sight |
| 107.33 | Visual observer |
| 107.35 | Operation of multiple aircraft |
| 107.37(a) | Yielding the right of way |
| 107.39 | Operation over people |
| 107.41 | Operation in certain airspace |
| 107.51 | Speed, altitude, visibility, and cloud clearance |
| 107.145 | Operations over moving vehicles |

Waivers of 107.25 and 107.31 may not be used to carry another person's property for compensation or hire.

## Rules That Cannot Be Waived

Anything not on the list. Examples:

- Carrying hazardous material (107.36)
- Alcohol and drugs (107.27)
- Registration
- Remote pilot certification

## How to Apply

Operational waiver applications are submitted through the FAA's **Aviation Safety Hub**. The FAA moved waiver applications there from FAADroneZone. Airspace authorizations did not move: they are still requested through LAANC or FAADroneZone.

## Common Traps

- "Any Part 107 rule can be waived with a good enough reason." Only the listed sections.
- "A waiver covers everything at the site." It covers only the sections it names. Controlled airspace still needs an authorization.
- "Night flight needs a waiver." Not since April 2021, unless you want relief from the lighting requirement.

lessons.title: Operations Over People and Remote ID
objectives: State when a small unmanned aircraft may be flown over people without a waiver
Distinguish the four categories and the limits on each
Apply the rules for open-air assemblies and moving vehicles
Explain declarations of compliance, labels, and remote pilot operating instructions
Describe the three ways to comply with Remote ID and what each broadcasts

sections.title: When You May Fly Over People
sections.content:
## The Baseline Rule (14 CFR 107.39)

No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft over a human being unless that person is:

1. **Directly participating** in the operation, or
2. Under a **covered structure** or inside a **stationary vehicle** that can provide reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft, or
3. The operation meets one of the **four categories** in Subpart D

Operating within a category needs **no waiver**. A waiver is needed only for an operation over people that fits none of the three cases.

## Remote Pilot Responsibilities

Before an operation over people, the remote PIC must confirm that the aircraft meets the requirements of the category being used (14 CFR 107.49) and choose an operating area that fits that category's limits.

## Two Terms to Know

**Open-air assembly:** the rule does not define the term. AC 107-2A gives examples such as sporting events, concerts, parades, protests, and community festivals.

**Sustained flight:** AC 107-2A describes it as hovering above people, flying back and forth over them, or circling above them. A brief, one-time transit that is incidental to a point-to-point flight is not sustained flight.

## Night

Subpart D does not limit operations over people to daytime. A night operation over people must meet the night rule (14 CFR 107.29) and the requirements of the category.

## Common Traps

- "Any flight over people needs a waiver." That was the rule before April 2021.
- "Telling people about the flight makes them participants." Notice does not make a bystander a direct participant.
- "A hard hat is reasonable protection." The rule names a covered structure or a stationary vehicle.

sections.title: The Four Categories
sections.content:
## The Four Categories

| | Category 1 | Category 2 | Category 3 | Category 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **What qualifies** | Weighs **0.55 lbs or less** on takeoff and throughout the flight, including everything on board or attached | Will not cause injury equal to or greater than a transfer of **11 foot-pounds** of kinetic energy from a rigid object | Will not cause injury equal to or greater than a transfer of **25 foot-pounds** of kinetic energy from a rigid object | Has an **airworthiness certificate** issued under 14 CFR Part 21 |
| **Exposed rotating parts** | None that would lacerate human skin | None that would lacerate human skin | None that would lacerate human skin | No Part 107 requirement |
| **Declaration of compliance and label** | Not required | **Required** | **Required** | Not required |
| **Open-air assemblies** | Sustained flight only if the operation is Remote ID compliant | Sustained flight only if the operation is Remote ID compliant | **No operations over open-air assemblies** | Sustained flight only if the operation is Remote ID compliant |

"Remote ID compliant" here means the operation meets 14 CFR 89.110 (standard Remote ID) or 89.115(a) (broadcast module).

Category 2 and 3 aircraft must also have no safety defects.

## Category 3: Extra Limits (14 CFR 107.125)

A Category 3 aircraft may fly over a person only if:

- The operation is within or over a **closed or restricted-access site**, and everyone on the site is **on notice** that a small unmanned aircraft may fly over them, **or**
- The aircraft does **not maintain sustained flight** over any person who is not directly participating or protected by a covered structure or stationary vehicle

## Category 4 (14 CFR 107.140)

The aircraft must be operated within the operating limitations in its FAA-approved Flight Manual, and those limitations must not prohibit operations over people. It has its own maintenance and recordkeeping requirements.

## How to Remember the Energy Limits

The lower number goes with the category that has fewer operating restrictions: **11 for Category 2, 25 for Category 3**.

## Common Traps

- "Category 2 is for aircraft under 0.55 lbs." That is Category 1. Category 2 has no weight test.
- "Category 1 can hover over a concert with no further conditions." Sustained flight over an open-air assembly requires Remote ID compliance.
- "Category 3 may cross a parade if it does not hover." Category 3 may not operate over open-air assemblies at all.
- "Weighing under 55 lbs qualifies an aircraft for a category." Weight under 55 lbs only makes it a small UAS.

sections.title: Operations Over Moving Vehicles
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR 107.145 covers flight over people inside **moving vehicles**.

**Categories 1, 2, and 3** may operate over people in moving vehicles only if:

- The aircraft stays within or over a **closed or restricted-access site**, and everyone inside a vehicle on the site is **on notice** that a small unmanned aircraft may fly over them, **or**
- The aircraft does **not maintain sustained flight** over moving vehicles

**Category 4** aircraft may do so if the operating limitations in the Flight Manual do not prohibit it.

## What This Means in Practice

- Crossing a public road without lingering over traffic: allowed for a category-eligible aircraft.
- Following a car down a public road: sustained flight over a moving vehicle, not allowed without a waiver.
- A film set on a closed road where every driver has been briefed: allowed.

Vehicle speed is not part of the rule.

## Common Traps

- "Flight over moving vehicles is always prohibited." It is allowed in the two situations above.
- "A stationary vehicle and a moving vehicle are treated the same." A person inside a stationary vehicle that gives reasonable protection is covered by the baseline rule in 107.39. Moving vehicles are covered by 107.145.

sections.title: Declarations, Labels, and Operating Instructions
sections.content:
## How an Aircraft Becomes Eligible for Category 2 or 3

1. **Means of compliance (14 CFR 107.155).** A method of showing the aircraft meets the injury and safety requirements, by test, analysis, or inspection. The FAA must accept it.
2. **Declaration of compliance (14 CFR 107.160).** The applicant declares that specific aircraft, by make, model, and serial number, meet the requirements using an accepted means of compliance. The FAA must accept the declaration.

The **applicant** is whoever designs, produces, or modifies the aircraft. That is usually the manufacturer, but a person who builds or modifies an aircraft can submit a declaration too. The FAA can rescind a declaration, and no one may operate an aircraft listed on a rescinded declaration over people.

## The Label

- A Category 2 or 3 aircraft must carry a label, **in English, legible, prominent, and permanently affixed**, showing the category or categories it is eligible for.
- If the label is damaged, destroyed, or missing, the **remote PIC must relabel the aircraft** before operating over people. The replacement must be in English, legible, prominent, and must stay on the aircraft for the duration of the operation (14 CFR 107.135).

## Remote Pilot Operating Instructions

The applicant must provide operating instructions with the aircraft. At a minimum they cover:

- A system description, including **required components**, limitations, and the declared category or categories
- **Modifications** that will not change the aircraft's ability to meet its category requirements
- How to verify and change the **mode or configuration**, if the aircraft has more than one

AC 107-2A explains that a modification the operating instructions do not allow means the aircraft no longer meets its category. The label does not keep a modified aircraft eligible.

## What the Remote Pilot Checks

- The aircraft is listed on an **FAA-accepted declaration of compliance** (the FAA publishes them)
- The correct **label** is on the aircraft
- The aircraft is in the configuration the operating instructions describe

## Category 4 Maintenance

A Category 4 aircraft must be maintained and inspected as 14 CFR 107.140 requires, using the manufacturer's instructions or other methods acceptable to the FAA. Maintenance records are kept for at least one year.

## Common Traps

- "The remote pilot files the declaration before each job." The applicant files it once for the aircraft model.
- "A worn-off label means the aircraft must go back to the manufacturer." The remote PIC may relabel it.
- "Removing the prop guards is fine if the label is still on." Not unless the operating instructions allow that configuration.

sections.title: Remote Identification
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

14 CFR Part 89 requires unmanned aircraft operated in U.S. airspace to comply with Remote Identification in one of three ways.

| Option | Rule | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Standard Remote ID aircraft | 89.110 | Remote ID is built into the aircraft |
| Remote ID broadcast module | 89.115(a) | An add-on module is attached to an aircraft that has no built-in Remote ID |
| FAA-recognized identification area (FRIA) | 89.115(b) | No Remote ID equipment, flown only inside a recognized area |

Remote ID is a **local broadcast** from the aircraft that nearby personal wireless devices can receive. It is not an internet service and it is not ADS-B.

## Standard Remote ID

- The aircraft must broadcast **from takeoff to shutdown**.
- If it stops broadcasting, the person at the controls must **land as soon as practicable**.
- The Remote ID equipment must be functional and must not be disabled.

It broadcasts these message elements (14 CFR 89.305):

1. The aircraft's identity: its serial number or a session ID
2. Latitude and longitude of the **control station**
3. Geometric altitude of the control station
4. Latitude and longitude of the **aircraft**
5. Geometric altitude of the aircraft
6. Velocity of the aircraft
7. A time mark
8. An indication of the aircraft's **emergency status**

## Broadcast Module

- The pilot must confirm the module is working **before takeoff**.
- The person manipulating the flight controls must be able to **see the aircraft at all times**.
- If the module stops broadcasting, the pilot must land as soon as practicable.

It broadcasts (14 CFR 89.315): the module's serial number, the aircraft's latitude, longitude, geometric altitude, and velocity, the latitude, longitude, and geometric altitude of the **takeoff location**, and a time mark.

## Standard Aircraft Versus Module

| | Standard Remote ID | Broadcast module |
|---|---|---|
| Location of the pilot | Control station location | **Takeoff location** instead |
| Emergency status | Yes | No |
| Must keep aircraft in sight | Part 107 line-of-sight rule applies | Required by Part 89 itself |

## FAA-Recognized Identification Areas

An aircraft with no Remote ID equipment may be flown only if the aircraft and the pilot **stay within the boundaries of the FRIA** and the pilot can **see the aircraft at all times**.

## Other Points

- **ADS-B Out** may not be used to meet the Remote ID requirement (14 CFR 89.125).
- The FAA may authorize operations without Remote ID for **aeronautical research** or to show compliance with regulations (14 CFR 89.120).
- The serial number of the standard Remote ID aircraft or the module must be listed on the aircraft's **registration**.
- A foreign-registered aircraft needs a **Confirmation of Identification** from the FAA before it is operated in the United States (14 CFR 89.130).
- Standard Remote ID aircraft and broadcast modules carry a **label** stating that they meet Part 89.

## Common Traps

- "Remote ID broadcasts the pilot's name and address." No personal information is broadcast.
- "A module lets you fly beyond line of sight." A module requires the aircraft to stay in sight.
- "If Remote ID fails in flight, finish the job and report it." Land as soon as practicable.

sections.title: Previously Manufactured sUAS
sections.content:
## What the Regulation Says

"Previously manufactured" refers to small UAS produced before the operations-over-people and Remote ID rules took effect in 2021.

## Operations Over People

- A previously manufactured aircraft can be used for ordinary Part 107 operations as before.
- To fly over people it must meet a category like any other aircraft.
- AC 107-2A explains that it can become eligible for Category 2 or 3 when an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance covers it. It must then be labeled, and the remote PIC may apply the label.
- Category 1 depends only on weight and exposed rotating parts, so a light enough aircraft qualifies without a declaration.

## Remote ID

A previously manufactured aircraft with no built-in Remote ID complies by:

1. Adding a Remote ID broadcast module, or
2. Operating only within a FAA-recognized identification area

## Key Facts

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Ordinary Part 107 operations | Unaffected |
| Operations over people | Only if the aircraft meets a category |
| Path to Category 2 or 3 | FAA-accepted declaration of compliance plus label |
| Remote ID | Broadcast module or FRIA |
